name: Algorithms and Data Structures: Quiz 2
grading_style:
Reasoning points need the reasoning on paper: a bare result gets only the result point.
Ignore spelling mistakes as long as the word is recognizable.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search, and why?
questions.answer_key: O(log n): each comparison discards half of the remaining interval, so after k steps n/2^k elements are left, and k = log2 n steps reach one element. It only works on a sorted array.

criteria.description: Explains that each step halves the search interval (discards half of the remaining elements).
hints: Re-read what you wrote, then look at what one comparison with the middle element tells you.
Think about how much of the search interval is left after each comparison.
Each comparison throws away half of what is left: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. How many steps does that take for n elements?

criteria.description: Says the array must be sorted.
hints: Look at the step where you compare with the middle element: what does it assume about the others?
Think about what being sorted lets you discard.
If the middle is smaller than the target and the array is sorted, everything to its left is smaller too. What happens to that step when the array is not sorted?

transfer.prompt: What would change in the algorithm if the array were sorted in descending order?

questions.prompt: A recursive function has no base case. What happens when it runs, and why?
questions.answer_key: It never stops calling itself and ends with a stack overflow, because every call pushes a new frame on the call stack until the stack's memory runs out.

criteria.description: Says it never stops and ends in a stack overflow (or a recursion error / crash).
hints: Re-read your answer: does the program ever get to stop on its own?
Think about the call stack and the fact that its size is limited.
Each call waits for the next one and none of them returns. How does that end?

criteria.description: Explains that every call adds a frame to the call stack until memory runs out.
hints: Re-read your answer: what does the computer have to remember every time the function calls itself?
Think about the call stack: what is stored on it for each call?
Every call puts a frame (its variables and where to return) on the call stack, and the stack has a fixed size. What happens after thousands of calls?

transfer.prompt: What would change if the function did have a base case, but the input never reached it?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give one real-world example of each.
questions.answer_key: A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO); a queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO). Examples: a pile of plates or an undo history; a line at a shop or a printer queue.

criteria.description: Stack is last-in-first-out (LIFO), queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO).
hints: Re-read your answer: which item comes out before the others in each one?
Think about the order items come out: the newest one or the oldest one?
In a stack the last item added leaves first (LIFO); in a queue the first item added leaves first (FIFO). Which one is which in your answer?

criteria.description: Gives a sensible real-world example of each.
hints: Re-read your answer and think of a place where people or things wait for their turn.
Think of everyday situations where the newest item is used first, and where the oldest is.
A pile of plates: you take the top one, the last put there. A line at a shop: the first in line is served first. What is one example of your own for each?

transfer.prompt: If a printer kept its jobs in a stack instead of a queue, what would happen to the first document sent?
